title: AI and developmental profiling reveal conserved rules for microRNA strand selection
summary: Using a high-throughput qPCR assay, Arizona State University researchers measured microRNA 5p/3p strand use across six Caenorhabditis elegans developmental stages and selected tissues. A machine-learning model trained on experimentally measured strand usage identified compositional and structural sequence features associated with strand preference; the learned relationships predicted strand usage in other vertebrates, including humans, and the authors report that the rules are conserved but context-dependent.
ai_technology: Predictive machine-learning model using 77 biologically informed features, trained on high-throughput qPCR measurements from the HiTmiSS platform
organization: Arizona State University Biodesign Institute and School of Life Sciences; Arizona State University School of Computing and Augmented Intelligence

evidence.tested: Using a high-throughput qPCR assay, Arizona State University researchers measured microRNA 5p/3p strand use across six Caenorhabditis elegans developmental stages and selected tissues.
evidence.unknown: The dataset measured strand usage in C. elegans across six developmental stages and specific tissues; cross-species including human results are model predictions/validation against available strand-usage data, not direct tests of gene-regulatory outcomes in human cells. The result concerns strand-selection patterns and predictors, not disease causality or therapeutic efficacy.
evidence.ai_role: The model learned strand-preference relationships from the experimental strand-usage dataset, quantified feature contributions, and predicted preference across additional nematode microRNAs and vertebrate species. Experimental qPCR measurements established the C. elegans profiles; predictions across species extend the analysis but are not themselves experimental confirmation of function in each organism.
